1. The animation shows inflation eroding a fixed income check. It uses US consumer prices (CPI-U) as an illustration. It compares each later check with the first check, in purchasing power and not in dollars. The labels say it covers US data only and is history, not a forecast.

2. A gold bar chart of purchasing power sits in all six frames. In frame 1 the chart is plain, with a note that each check is compared with its own first check. In frames 2 to 4 a bright highlight sweeps across the chart. Text appears that says, "1990s starts: 0 of 120 kept up, typical 94.8%." It also says, "2000 to Aug 2006: 0 of 79, best 99.5%." In frame 5 a purple label reads "Ruth: 90.4%," and a small purple figure stands at the right edge of the chart. In frame 6 the text fades out.

3. The numbers suggest that a fixed, non-inflation-adjusted payment lost purchasing power over time. In the periods shown, none of the 120 retirements that started in the 1990s kept up with prices. The same is true of none of the 79 that started from 2000 to August 2006. The typical retiree ended with about 94.8% of the starting purchasing power, and even the best case was 99.5%, which is still under 100%. "Ruth" appears to be an example retiree whose check was worth about 90.4% of its starting value, so roughly 10% of its buying power was gone.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might reasonably take away that a level payout loses buying power. A payout that adjusts for inflation, or other resources to cover rising prices, might be worth weighing for my own quote. But the animation doesn't say that, and it also doesn't say how much those options cost.

5. The takeaway in 4 is my own conclusion. The animation only presented the data and labeled it illustrative history, not a forecast.
